source: Vessey (1985) Expertise in debugging computer programs: a process analysis
finding: Sixteen COBOL programmers (8 expert, 8 novice) debugged one program aloud. Experts were defined after the fact by chunking ability, not job tenure.
numbers: N=16, one COBOL program, high or low bug (4+4 per group). Ex post chunking classification explained 73.7% of variance in debug time vs 36.1% for manager ratings. Only 10 of 16 subjects were classed the same by both methods.
limits: Small N, one program. Expert label is built from performance, so it is partly circular. Author says reliability of the classification is untested (no test-retest).
agent_relevance: Skill is a property of the process, not of seniority. A scaffold should score its own steps by what they do, not by who ran them.

source: Vessey (1985) Expertise in debugging computer programs: a process analysis
finding: Experts were faster and made fewer mistakes. Time to find the error and total debug time both favoured experts.
numbers: Mean debug time 15 min 40 s experts vs 28 min 3 s novices (ANOVA p<0.001). Time to error p=0.005. Mistakes (wrong repairs): novices more (p=0.005); all 5 programmers with wrong fixes were novices. Low bug took longer than high bug (p=0.001).
limits: Mistakes were few (8 in total, 6 on the low bug). Class was derived partly from these same outcomes.
agent_relevance: Wrong fixes cluster in the weak debuggers. A confirm step after repair is where the loss shows up.

source: Vessey (1985) Expertise in debugging computer programs: a process analysis
finding: Novices went through more problem-solving phases and episodes, but each episode lasted as long as for experts. Novices reread the same module more.
numbers: Novices more major phases (p=0.001) and episodes (p=0.003); average time per episode no difference. Modules examined: novices more (p=0.045). Times the faulty module B000 was examined: novices more (p=0.007).
limits: Counts are tied to the ex post classification, which used position changes.
agent_relevance: Weak debugging looks like churn between places, not slower thinking. Count re-visits as an impasse signal.

source: Vessey (1985) Expertise in debugging computer programs: a process analysis
finding: Strategy rather than speed separated the groups. Two conditions fit 15 of 16 subjects: breadth-first search that keeps hypotheses open, and system thinking (a model of program structure and a causal model of the error).
numbers: Decision table of two binary conditions classified 15 of 16 subjects as the chunking-based classification did. Subjects followed 6 of 16 possible strategy paths. Programmers constrained by their own early hypotheses were novices.
quote: They do not permit the formulation of hypotheses to lead them to a depth-first search for the error.
limits: Four-factor tree built after the fact on 16 subjects; not tested on new people. NH2 did not fit.
agent_relevance: Supports S5: locate by building a model first, and do not lock onto the first hypothesis (G1, G2).

source: Vessey (1985) Expertise in debugging computer programs: a process analysis
finding: Things that did NOT discriminate: looking at the output first, reading modules in order vs mentally executing, and doing a familiarity phase before or after finding the error.
numbers: Table 9 (familiarity/exploration before detection): no consistent pattern between groups. Module procedure: experts 5 lexical, 2 execution; novices 2 lexical, 4 execution, but author states this had no effect on problem solving. Number of data-division items: no difference. Number of hypotheses: novices more (p=0.045).
quote: Directed search for the solution ... is not a determinant of debugging expertise.
limits: Null results from N=16; low power. Cannot rule out small effects.
agent_relevance: Do not hard-code 'read output first' or 'trace first' as the right order. Either can work. What matters is how hypotheses are held.

source: Vessey (1985) Expertise in debugging computer programs: a process analysis
finding: Vessey describes five phases in every protocol: determine the problem, gain familiarity, explore, evaluate to a hypothesis, repair. Strategic goals go down to tactical and operational goals.
numbers: Strategic goals: determine problem; understand function and structure; locate error; repair and confirm. Every protocol had problem determination and repair; other phases varied.
limits: Descriptive model fitted to 16 protocols of one task type (batch COBOL, control-break bug).
agent_relevance: Matches the S-states closely: restate, understand, locate, then S5 revise. Gives a phase vocabulary for logs.

source: Gould (1975) Some psychological evidence on how people debug computer programs
finding: Earlier founding study. Ten experienced programmers debugged 12 FORTRAN listings, each with one non-syntactic bug. Results replicated Gould and Drongowski (1974).
numbers: N=10, 12 listings. Median debug time about 7 min; 11% of listings had the bug not found; fewer than 1 wrong claim of location per listing. Assignment-statement bugs about 3x harder to find than array or interaction bugs. Debugging about 3x more efficient on programs debugged before (with a different bug). Subjects rarely used interactive debug tools.
limits: From abstract record via search only; full text not read. 1970s batch FORTRAN.
agent_relevance: Repeat exposure to the same code makes locating much faster: a case for keeping a model of the program across turns. Bug type matters more than the person.

source: Katz and Anderson (1987) Debugging: an analysis of bug-location strategies
finding: Four experiments on students debugging LISP. Students can usually fix a bug once they find it; the hard part is locating the faulty line. Strategy depends on whether the program is their own or someone else's.
numbers: Four experiments (sample sizes not read). Search results restate the abstract only.
quote: students can usually fix a bug once they locate it
limits: Abstract-level only; page could not be fetched. Students, LISP, 1980s.
agent_relevance: Same split as Tyen 2023 and Olausson 2023 for LLMs: locating is the bottleneck, repair is cheap. Supports locate-before-fix.

source: Gugerty and Olson (1986) Debugging by skilled and novice programmers (CHI '86)
finding: Two experiments (LOGO, Pascal). Experts debug faster and more accurately, spend more time on comprehension and build a fuller program representation, and form accurate hypotheses sooner. Novices lack knowledge to form good hypotheses and add new bugs.
numbers: Numbers not read. Secondary summary says experts and novices distributed their activities in the same way.
limits: Summary only; I did not open the paper. Treat claims as unverified.
agent_relevance: Same direction as Vessey: comprehension first, and bad repairs come from novices. Supports a comprehension step before locate.

source: Parnin and Orso (2011) Are automated debugging techniques actually helping programmers?
finding: A fault-localisation ranking tool (Tarantula) did not speed up the harder task. It helped only the top performers on the easy task.
numbers: Main run N=24 students (tool vs none); follow-up N=10; pilot N=34 total. Tetris: 12:42 tool vs 14:14 no tool, not significant. NanoXML: 20:16 vs 22:30, not significant. High performers (N=10) Tetris 8:51 vs 14:28, p<0.05. Completions: 18 Tetris vs 10 NanoXML.
limits: Students, two tasks, small groups. The group labels in Table 1 are hard to read from the extracted text. Later work (Xia 2016) found the opposite.
agent_relevance: Handing the agent a ranked suspect list is not enough on its own. A 'show the model the real output' step may matter more than a ranking.

source: Parnin and Orso (2011) Are automated debugging techniques actually helping programmers?
finding: Rank of the faulty line did not matter much. People do not walk a ranked list in order, and they do not recognise a bug just by seeing the line.
numbers: Moving faulty line from rank 7 to 35 (Tetris) or 83 to 16 (NanoXML), N=10 follow-up: no significant effect; Tetris-to-NanoXML time ratio 0.79 in both groups. 37% of list visits skipped more than one position (average skip 10). Average 10.3 direction changes per person. Only 1 of 10 stopped after clicking the fault; they spent about 61% of their time after first seeing it.
quote: participants spent (or wasted) on average 61% of their time continuing to inspect statements
limits: Small N. Rank change test N=10.
agent_relevance: 'Perfect bug understanding' is false: seeing the fault is not understanding it. The agent needs an explain step after locate, not just a pointer (G2).

source: Parnin and Orso (2011) Are automated debugging techniques actually helping programmers?
finding: Observation: tool users fixed the real fault; some non-tool users patched around the failure.
numbers: Several Tetris participants in the traditional groups edited the rotation code to bypass the failure; none of the ranking-tool users did.
limits: Anecdotal count, not tested.
agent_relevance: Symptom patches pass the visible check but are wrong. This is the G3 case: need a check that was not fitted to.

source: Xia, Bao, Lo and Li (2016) 'Automated debugging considered harmful' considered harmful
finding: Failed replication of Parnin and Orso's null result with professionals and real bugs: an accurate fault-localisation tool made people faster and more successful.
numbers: 36 professionals, 16 real bugs from 4 projects, 12 per group, 4 bugs each (48 per group). Success 98% accurate tool vs 77% no tool. Mean time 11.38 vs 26.45 min (Wilcoxon p=1.3e-10). Mediocre tool (fault at rank 6-10): 94% success, 16.35 min vs 26.45 (p=1.0e-5, Cliff's delta 0.5456, large).
limits: Authors built the study around fixed fault ranks. Professionals were recruited and may be atypical. Time counted only for successful fixes.
agent_relevance: Moderators are expertise, task realism and tool quality. A cheap localiser can be worth its cost with strong users; do not generalise from one null.

source: Xia, Bao, Lo and Li (2016) 'Automated debugging considered harmful' considered harmful
finding: Rank effects partly replicate: people check the top few ranks first and rank still matters in this study.
numbers: 75% of 24 participants visited the top 5 suspicious statements in sequence; only 33% did so for the top 6. Survey: 73.58% of 386 practitioners say a tool is successful if the fault is in the top 5.
limits: Order-following here conflicts with Parnin and Orso (37% of visits skipped).
agent_relevance: Conflicting findings on whether people follow rankings. Rank 1-5 matters; beyond that it is searched by intuition.

source: Alaboudi and LaToza (2020) Using hypotheses as a debugging aid
finding: Developers hold few hypotheses and most are wrong. Having a correct hypothesis early strongly predicts success.
numbers: Within-subjects, 20 developers, 3 tasks (60 sessions). Control stage-two hypotheses: 3 of 27 correct (11%). 20 of 60 sessions failed to fix. Correct hypothesis predicts fix (p=0.01). Six of the 20 failures had a correct hypothesis but a wrong fix.
limits: N=20, lab, web-app tasks (JavaScript/HTML). Correlation inside the study.
agent_relevance: Forming a correct hypothesis is the hard step; repair after it still fails sometimes (cause understood, fix not). Keep locate and repair as separate steps.

source: Alaboudi and LaToza (2020) Using hypotheses as a debugging aid
finding: Two aids compared: fault locations did nothing; potential hypotheses helped a lot.
numbers: Fault locations: no effect on correct hypotheses (stage two p=0.4125, stage three p=0.1320) or fix rate (p=0.6710); odds ratio 1.4, p=0.64. Potential hypotheses: odds ratio 6.24 (p=0.03) for success, larger than one year of experience (OR 1.14, p=0.04). No difference in time (p=0.61).
quote: developers who received potential hypotheses were six times more likely to fix the defect
limits: N=20; small cell counts (e.g. 4/8, 2/6). Wide confidence interval likely. Time not improved.
agent_relevance: Hypothesis lists beat line pointers. For the agent: offer candidate causes with evidence, not just a suspect line. G1 stays: only after a failing check.

source: Alaboudi and LaToza (2021) An exploratory study of debugging episodes
finding: In real work, debugging is frequent and uneven: many short episodes, and most debugging time sits in a few long ones that mix many activities.
numbers: 15 live-streamed sessions, 11 professionals, 30 h; 2137 debugging and 1407 programming activities. Debugging once every 8 min of programming; episode time share 48% of session (sd 24%, range 13-95%). Reported defects took 51 (sd 38) min vs 6 (sd 8) min for self-created ones. 14% of new-defect episodes ended without a fix. Coding agreement 75% episodes, 84% activities.
limits: Streamers are volunteers and may not represent typical work. Coded by the authors.
agent_relevance: Do not model debugging as one fixed pipeline: time is heavy-tailed. A budget cap and an escalate-to-impasse rule fit that shape.

source: Alaboudi and LaToza (2021) An exploratory study of debugging episodes
finding: No single activity dominates debugging time; debugging and coding look alike in what developers do (editing, browsing).
numbers: Browsing a file about 7 times per episode, 12% of episode time; 3 distinct files per episode; 67% of browsed files were later edited in the same episode. 20% of episodes lasted tens of minutes.
limits: Observational; no tool-use control.
agent_relevance: No special 'debug mode' activity set to copy; the difference is the goal structure, not the actions.

source: Olausson et al. (2024) Is self-repair a silver bullet for code generation?
finding: Self-repair gains are modest once cost is counted, and the bottleneck is the quality of the model's own feedback on its code.
numbers: HumanEval and APPS (300 APPS tasks: 180 interview, 60 competition, 60 intro). GPT-4 on APPS: gains up to 8% over a budget-matched baseline; GPT-3.5: marginal, up to 34% relative gain on competition-level only. Some settings show no gain.
limits: Old models (gpt-3.5-0301, gpt-4-0314, CodeLlama-13b). Budget matched by sample count, not wall time.
agent_relevance: Repair is not free: compare against just sampling again. Budget-match every claim.

source: Olausson et al. (2024) Is self-repair a silver bullet for code generation?
finding: Better feedback is the lever. Stronger-model feedback and human feedback raised repair success; humans were far better than GPT-4.
numbers: 16 participants gave 2 explanations each for 40 failing GPT-4 programs; 25 repair samples per feedback. Repair success overall: GPT-4 feedback 33.30%, human feedback 52.60%. By level: intro 42.64 vs 62.21; interview 19.33 vs 45.67; competition 3.67 vs 14.67.
limits: One-hour online task, N=16. Human effort and cost not measured.
agent_relevance: Locating and explaining the fault is the weak step for models, as Vessey's strategies predict for novices. Matches G2: feed real failing output plus a good diagnosis.

source: Tyen et al. (2024) LLMs cannot find reasoning errors, but can correct them given the error location
finding: Split self-correction into finding and fixing. Models are poor at finding the mistaken step but good at fixing it if told where.
numbers: BIG-Bench Mistake, 5 tasks, 300 traces each (85% incorrect, 15% correct). GPT-4 best overall mistake-finding accuracy only 52.87% (direct step prompting); GPT-3.5-Turbo as low as 1.67-19% on some tasks. Gemini Pro and PaLM 2 Unicorn also weak.
limits: Reasoning traces (word sorting, logic, arithmetic, Dyck, shuffled objects), not code. Traces were generated by PaLM 2.
agent_relevance: Direct support for locate-before-fix: the location, not the repair, is what is missing. Code should supply the location (G2).

source: Tyen et al. (2024) LLMs cannot find reasoning errors, but can correct them given the error location
finding: Given the true mistake location, backtracking helps; given a random location it still helps some but less, and it hurts correct traces.
numbers: Gain on originally incorrect answers, oracle vs random location: tracking shuffled objects +23.53 vs +11.76; multistep arithmetic +43.92 vs +20.39; Dyck +36.86 vs +21.57. Loss on originally correct traces about -6.7 to -11.4 (oracle), -8.9 to -15.9 (random).
limits: Oracle locations are not available at run time. A small trained classifier needed about 60-70% accuracy to pay off.
agent_relevance: A false alarm costs correct answers. Only revise when a check fails (G1, G3).

source: Huang et al. (2024) Large language models cannot self-correct reasoning yet
finding: Without external feedback, intrinsic self-correction does not help reasoning and often hurts. Earlier reported gains came from using the true answer to decide when to stop.
numbers: With oracle labels: GSM8K 75.9 to 95.5 (GPT-3.5 row) and 84.3 to 97.5 (GPT-4 row); HotpotQA 26.0 to 49.0 and 29.0 to 59.0. Intrinsic (no oracle) results fell. GPT-3.5 kept its first GSM8K answer 74.7% of the time and changed correct to incorrect more often than the reverse.
quote: The fundamental issue is that LLMs cannot properly judge the correctness of their reasoning.
limits: Reasoning QA, not code. Table row labels in my text extraction were mixed; read the paper for the exact assignment of rows.
agent_relevance: Core support for G1/G2: no revision from the model's opinion alone; require real output.

source: Chen et al. (2024) Teaching large language models to self-debug
finding: Debugging prompts that add unit-test execution give the largest gains. Explaining code in words (rubber duck) gives smaller gains without tests.
numbers: With unit tests: TransCoder Codex 80.4 baseline to 92.5; GPT-4 77.3 to about 90. MBPP Codex 61.4 to about 70; GPT-4 72.8 to about 80. Spider (no tests): Codex 81.3 to 84.1 with explanation. GPT-4 gain over 12% on TransCoder, 8% on MBPP.
limits: Mostly Codex, GPT-3.5, GPT-4 from 2023. Table cell alignment in my text extraction is partly uncertain, so values marked 'about' are approximate.
agent_relevance: Execution result is the key ingredient, not the model's own talk. Matches Vessey: the data in the task, not early belief, drives good debugging.

source: Chen et al. (2024) Teaching large language models to self-debug
finding: Without real code execution the gains mostly vanish and models grow overconfident in their first answer.
numbers: Table 3 (no execution): GPT-4 MBPP 72.8 to 76.4 with trace (+3.6); TransCoder GPT-4 77.3 to 78.4 (+1.1). Codex without tests: up to +5. MBPP Codex 'Simple' feedback fell from 61.4 to 57.6.
quote: models tend to be overconfident in their own initial predictions
limits: Self-judged feedback; GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 barely changed in several cells.
agent_relevance: Self-reported verification is unreliable. Run the code (G3).

source: Zhong, Wang and Shang (2024) Debug like a human: LDB
finding: Showing the model runtime values block by block beats having it imagine a dry run, and block-level beats both line-level and function-level.
numbers: HumanEval with seeds from GPT-3.5 / GPT-4 / Reflexion: baseline 73.8 / 87.2 / 91.5. Self-Debug (GPT-3.5) +7.3 / +1.2 / +0.6; LDB +9.1 / +2.4 / +3.6 (reaches 95.1 on Reflexion seeds). Gains up to 9.8% across HumanEval, MBPP, TransCoder. Block-level had best accuracy at lowest token cost; function-level needed about 8.1 iterations.
limits: GPT-3.5 as debugger backbone; HumanEval near ceiling for strong seeds. Visible tests used. No human baseline.
agent_relevance: Stepwise state inspection is a machine version of locating. Good fit for S5 if a trace is available.

source: Xia et al. (2024) Agentless: demystifying LLM-based software engineering agents
finding: A fixed three-step pipeline (localise, repair, validate) with no agent loop matched or beat open-source agents on SWE-bench Lite at lower cost.
numbers: SWE-bench Lite: 96 of 300 resolved (32.00%) at $0.70 per issue with GPT-4o. Localisation is hierarchical (file, then function, then line), mixing LLM and retrieval. Authors found SWE-bench Lite problems with the exact patch in the issue text and built a cleaned Lite-S.
limits: 2024 snapshot; the same table lists higher agent scores. Benchmark leakage risk noted by the authors.
agent_relevance: Locate-then-repair as a fixed program-controlled flow is competitive. Evidence for code deciding transitions (SCHEMA section 1).

source: Tian et al. (2024) DebugBench: evaluating debugging capability of LLMs
finding: On 4,253 bugs (C++, Java, Python), difficulty depends on bug type: syntax and reference bugs are easy, logic and multiple-bug cases are hard. Models are below humans.
numbers: DebugBench 4,253 instances, 4 major and 18 minor bug types; 2 commercial and 4 open models, zero-shot. Examples: logic 'operation error' gpt-4 68.6 vs human 10/12; syntax 'missing colons' gpt-4 93.6, human 12/12. Humans take about 20 min per bug; models under 10 s.
quote: Syntax and reference errors are comparatively simpler ... logic bugs pose a greater challenge
limits: Bugs implanted by GPT-4 into LeetCode code; human results are counts out of 12. Possible training-data overlap.
agent_relevance: Bug type is a major moderator. A scaffold should route logic bugs to a stronger localise-and-explain path.

source: Tian et al. (2024) DebugBench: evaluating debugging capability of LLMs
finding: Runtime feedback is not always helpful: it helps syntax and reference bugs but can hurt logic bugs.
numbers: Figure 4: traceback improves syntax and reference error fixing for gpt-4 and gpt-3.5-turbo and reduces logic error fixing. Multiple sampling (1 to 4) helps logic bugs.
quote: the details provided in traceback messages are often too low-level to facilitate effective debugging
limits: Measured with LeetCode test-suite messages; exact deltas are only in a figure I could not read from text.
agent_relevance: Raw tracebacks are not a universal fix. Pick the useful part and pair it with a hypothesis (G2).

source: Kang, Chen, Yoo and Lou (2025) Explainable automated debugging via LLM-driven scientific debugging (AutoSD)
finding: A hypothesis, experiment, observe, conclude loop with a real debugger gives repair performance competitive with baselines, and the model can signal when it is confident.
numbers: Where a plausible patch existed and the model emitted <DONE>, 89% were correct vs 82% without <DONE>. With debugger output hallucinated by the LLM, <DONE> solutions became 11 points less likely to be plausible (vs +12.4 points with real execution); individual-run plausible rate 73% with debugger vs 63% without.
limits: Benchmarks ARHE, Defects4J, BugsInPy. Gains are over baselines from 2023.
agent_relevance: A direct LLM version of Vessey's hypothesis-testing loop, and it works only with real execution (G2, G3).

source: Kang, Chen, Yoo and Lou (2025) Explainable automated debugging via LLM-driven scientific debugging (AutoSD)
finding: Human study on patch review: explanations improved judgement of patch correctness but did not change review time.
numbers: 20 participants (6 professionals), 6 bugs (3 ARHE, 3 BugsInPy), each bug reviewed by 10 people. More accurate with explanations in 5 of 6 bugs; Mann-Whitney U p<0.05. Two cases got worse (ARHE105, BIP003). 70% wanted explanations; 55% were satisfied with the format.
limits: N=20, mixed students and professionals; only patch review, not debugging from scratch.
agent_relevance: Explanations can raise accuracy of a human check but can also mislead in a minority of cases. A scaffold should still run the tests.
